title: Destroyer of Worlds
author: Larry Correia
review:
Great series that respects your time.

Kind of tough to rate this one because the beginning was sort of 3/5 and solid but slow to get rolling but the ending climax and falling action was amazing and makes me want to pick up the next one immediately. Seriously had one of the best duels I've read and he showed that he can do larger scale action well.

This series overall has a lot of heart, the characters all have good and often conflicting motivations, and the dialog has the right amount of humor and weight.

The world building is also well done and has enough mystery to keep me engaged, feels like it is unique in the fantasy genre. Very curious to see where things go.

“If your men respect you, they will carry you. Unless you are the incompetent coward I suspect you to be, then they’ll leave you for the buzzards and tell their rescuers you perished by my hand.”

“I am Ashok Vadal, you imbeciles. I am here to save your stupid lives. Warriors are coming from the west to kill you. Stay out of my way so I can kill them first!”
“I am Thakoor here. Thus I cannot make mistakes. Anything I say becomes true, because of the act of my saying it.”

“If you treat them as children, they will remain children. You must impose order on them. Every man must have a place.”

It was one thing to plot the destruction and rebuilding of the very fabric of their society, but Omand doubted even his most steadfast associates would follow him on his mission to enslave their ancient gods. Omand’s quest sounded mad, even to himself at times, but he could not deny what he had seen, and in the darkest forgotten corners of Lok he had laid his eyes upon strange things that no other man alive had ever seen.

Upheaval leads to death, starvation, disease, so on and so forth. But in the grand scheme of things, destruction is necessary. Old forests must burn so new trees can grow, then we cut those trees down to build houses, then we raze those houses to erect mansions. Every time man builds, first we must destroy. The demons destroyed the old world, and we made a new one ruled by kings. Then we destroyed that world to make the Law. Destruction is a bloody mess, but a necessary one. You must destroy one world before you can create a new one. Creation and destruction…One cannot exist without the other.

All this beauty…” He gestured at the expensive artwork which covered the walls. “It’s not for our enjoyment. It’s to establish to our inferiors how important we are, how much better we are than them, so that they will continue to allow us to manage their lives.”

I can’t by definition be unjust, because I’m the one who decides what the Law means in this land. Justice is whatever I say it is.

“Sorry about slugging you in the gut earlier,” said the guard next to Jagdish as he unlocked the shackles. “But, brother, I’ve got to say that was the most intense promotion ceremony I’ve ever been to!”
Devedas had asked him to protect Rada. That obligation didn’t end simply because he’d been bitten by a tiger, stabbed six times, and then been left for dead facedown in a lake.

“What was meant as punishment turned out to be a reward. They made you my obligation. You became my reason to live.” A woman made of stone had let herself be vulnerable long enough for a black-hearted killer to learn what it meant to be kind. Then their time together was over.
In a world where every man had his mandated place, those in charge could never let the weak have a tool which enabled them to so effortlessly match the strong.

That had been Devedas’ greatest fear, for never in the world had there been a man of more singular will than Ashok Vadal. And now he had found something else to believe in. “I am truly sorry it must end this way, Ashok.” Devedas was somber. “Me too.” Ashok reached up and put his mask back on. “Let us begin.”
Yet he would fight without reluctance for Ashok truly wished to live. For that to happen, Protectors would have to die. So be it.
“What good is the word of a criminal?” “It is all I can offer. Accept it, or all of you can go beneath the hooves of my cavalry.”

There’re too many pigs feeding at the trough and new piglets born every day. There’s too much rot. It’s all crumbling. Eventually it will fail. Better to do it now, while the good parts can be saved.

I failed.”

Ashok realized they were somehow over two hundred feet from where they’d started from, and the sky had grown dark and angry with storm clouds. Where did the time go when you were trying to kill your best friend?

Jagdish paid no attention to such things. His life was a bittersweet parody of what he’d worked for. There was duty to focus on, and in the hours he wasn’t fulfilling that duty his life was empty, cold, and gray.
How are you alive?” “I’m beginning to suspect I can’t die.”
